title: AcceptanceContract
description: Acceptance criteria are the contract (PLAN.md §7). A criterion is a deterministic action sequence plus one or more declarative expectations over the resulting observation.

description.description: Documentation only. Optional on purpose: a field that provably cannot change a verdict must never be the reason a run stops to ask a human.

mandatory.description: A run can only be PASS when every mandatory criterion passes. Optional criteria are reported but never gate the verdict.

steps.description: Deterministic actions executed in order before observation. A criterion with no steps validates the landing state.

evidence.description: Artifacts that must exist for this criterion to be satisfiable. Absence of a required artifact means the run is not PASS (PLAN.md §32, M5).

Step.description: Exactly one action key per step.

sql.description: One statement put to the database, producing the result set the criterion's `db.value` expectations read. This is how a database world is acted on: it has no page to click and no form to fill, so the equivalent of an interaction is a query with an observable result.

apply.description: One manifest submitted to the cluster the world stands in for, producing the objects the criterion's `k8s.*` expectations read. This is how a cluster world is acted on: it has no page to click and no form to fill, so the equivalent of an interaction is a manifest with an observable result. The path is read relative to the application directory, so the criterion judges the manifests the application actually ships rather than a copy embedded in the contract.

run.description: One command executed inside the system the world stands in for, as an argument vector rather than a command line, producing the files, permissions, users, services and ports the criterion's `posix.*` expectations read. This is how a system world is acted on: it has no page to click and no form to fill, so the equivalent of an interaction is a command with an observable result. An argument vector rather than a shell string because a shell string would need a shell, and the shell would be a second substitution with its own quoting rules to get wrong - while the interesting question (can this user read that file?) is asked perfectly well by naming the program and its arguments. The world resolves the program name against its own bin directory, so the same record drives a substituted system and a real one.

method.description: The HTTP method. Upper case; a document may write any case and the loader normalises it, so the world has one spelling of each method.

path.description: The path of the request, resolved by the substitute against the account it stands in for, so a criterion can name a path without knowing which host answered.

body.description: The request body, when there is one. A string rather than a nested document, because an object store's PUT body IS the object's contents - requiring a contract to nest bytes inside a JSON object to make them expressible would make the common case the awkward one. `null` means no body, and is written out rather than omitted so a reader of the adapter's record can tell a decision from a dropped field.

validator.description: A registered validator name, e.g. web.ui.text. An unregistered name is an unresolvable_entity ambiguity, caught before execution.

target.description: A selector for target-based validators, or a URL for web.ui.url.

message.description: Human-readable failure text shown in latest-failure.md.
